Copy First, Translate Later: Interpreting Translation Dynamics
in Multilingual Pretraining

Felicia Körner Affiliation: MaiNLP, Center for Information and Language Processing, LMU Munich, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Machine Learning (MCML)    Maria Matveev Affiliation: Munich Center for Machine Learning (MCML) Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, LMU Munich, Germany    Florian Eichin Affiliation: MaiNLP, Center for Information and Language Processing, LMU Munich, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Machine Learning (MCML)    Gitta Kutyniok Affiliation: Munich Center for Machine Learning (MCML) Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, LMU Munich, Germany Affiliation: Department of Physics and Technology, University of Tromsø, Norway Affiliation: DLR-German Aerospace Center, Germany    Barbara Plank Affiliation: MaiNLP, Center for Information and Language Processing, LMU Munich, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Machine Learning (MCML)    Michael A. Hedderich Affiliation: MaiNLP, Center for Information and Language Processing, LMU Munich, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Machine Learning (MCML)    *Equal contribution. Shared senior authorship. Correspondence: f.koerner@lmu.de
Abstract

Large language models exhibit impressive cross-lingual capabilities. However, prior work analyzes this phenomenon through isolated factors and at sparse points during training, limiting our understanding of how cross-lingual generalization emerges—particularly in the early phases of learning. To study the early trajectory of linguistic and translation capabilities, we pretrain a multilingual 1.7B model on nine diverse languages, capturing checkpoints at a much finer granularity. We further introduce a novel word-level translation dataset and trace how translation develops over training through behavioral analyses, model-component analysis, and parameter-based ablations. We find that the model quickly acquires basic linguistic capabilities in parallel with token-level copying, while translation develops in two distinct phases: an initial phase dominated by copying and surface-level similarities, and a second phase in which more generalizing translation mechanisms are developed while copying is refined. Together, these findings provide a fine-grained view of how cross-lingual generalization develops during multilingual pretraining.

1 Introduction

Cross-lingual transfer is a key property of multilingual large language models, allowing high-resource languages to benefit lower-resourced ones Wu and Dredze (2019); Patil et al. (2022). Surprisingly, cross-lingual transfer arises even without explicit cross-lingual supervision, such as parallel training data or cross-lingual training objectives Blevins and Zettlemoyer (2022), a phenomenon we refer to as incidental cross-lingual transfer. Prior work has identified contributing factors, such as vocabulary overlap Kallini et al. (2025), incidental parallel data Briakou et al. (2023), and shared intermediate representation spaces Wendler et al. (2024). However, how the mechanisms behind this phenomenon emerge are poorly understood.

We argue that studying the final model alone cannot explain why the mechanisms underlying cross-lingual transfer arise and how they interact. Instead, we trace their emergence and interplay over the course of pretraining. To this end, we pretrain a multilingual 1.71.7B model on a mix of data from nine typologically diverse languages, and capture a particularly high checkpoint density. We use word-level translation as a testbed for cross-lingual transfer for which we construct a novel word-level translation dataset.

Our evaluation shows that in the very early stages of training, word-level translation is enabled by token11 1 We use “token” to refer to a subword unit produced by a tokenizer, historically also referred to as “subtoken”. overlap, while at the same time the model frequently erroneously copies tokens. We identify two phases of learning: Phase I, in which the model rapidly acquires linguistic knowledge and a useful, but overeager copying mechanism, and Phase II, in which the model develops translation aided by token overlap, and, more slowly, the ability to translate without token overlap (see Fig. 1). We hypothesize these phases to reflect an emergence and interplay of two mechanisms: token-level copying Feucht et al. (2025), and a generalizing mechanism implementing shared representation spaces Wendler et al. (2024). The interplay between these mechanisms raises two questions: how does the model learn to translate without shared tokens, and how does it learn to prefer translation over copying where they diverge?

We study the training dynamics of these mechanisms, combining data attribution, model component analysis, and parameter-based ablation, to offer a unified view of cross-lingual transfer. Our analysis sheds light on how the copying mechanism emerges and refines, how the model develops the generalizing mechanism enabling translation without overlap, and how it learns to prefer translation over copying.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    Pretraining checkpoints of a multilingual 1.71.7B model,​22 2 On publication, we will release our word-level translation dataset, code, and checkpoints to facilitate future work. more fine-grained (every 185185M tokens) and capturing earlier training than any other publicly available multilingual checkpoints.

  • •

    A novel, carefully curated word-level translation dataset across 72 language pairs, stratified over PoS tag and English word frequency, and including a set of language-pair specific valid translations.​22footnotemark: 2

  • •

    A behavioral analysis of word-level translation and basic linguistic capabilities over early multilingual pretraining, identifying two main phases of learning.

  • •

    A comprehensive interpretability study attributing this behavior to the pretraining data and model components, uncovering the emergence and interplay of two central mechanisms: a useful, albeit overeager copying mechanism, which emerges and refines over training, and a generalizing mechanism which enables cross-lingual transfer.

2 Related Work

A rich body of work investigates cross-lingual transfer, identifying beneficial factors such as similar morphology and syntax, and lexical overlap Philippy et al. (2023); Hämmerl et al. (2024). A highly relevant beneficial factor to our work is token overlap Wu and Dredze (2019); Patil et al. (2022); Limisiewicz et al. (2023); Bagheri Nezhad et al. (2025). Kallini et al. (2025) study the function of token overlap, training bilingual models with varying levels of overlap between the monolingual corpora, finding that even semantically dissimilar shared tokens aid transfer. Feucht et al. (2025) provide a mechanistic account, identifying token induction heads and concept induction heads, with the latter critical for word-level translation.

Token overlap does not explain how transfer occurs across languages with limited shared vocabulary. A complementary line of work suggests that transfer is mediated by generalizing mechanisms implementing shared internal representations. Wendler et al. (2024) find evidence for a shared “concept space” distinct from language-specific input and output representations. Dumas et al. (2025) provide causal evidence, demonstrating that concept and language are encoded independently in latent representations.

Finally, in contrast to previous work that only studies trained models, we argue for studying training dynamics in order to understand the emergence of incidental cross-lingual transfer. Studies in this vein are hampered by the limited availability of multilingual checkpoints, which, if released at all, are typically sparse and provide incomplete information about pretraining data (cf. Apertus et al., 2025). Riemenschneider and Frank (2025) and Zeng et al. (2025) focus primarily on BLOOM BigScience Workshop (2022), while Körner et al. (2026) focus on EuroLLM 1.71.7B. All three studies focus on the development of cross-lingual shared neurons or shared internal representations.

By contrast, we pretrain our own model, giving us fine-grained checkpoint density and control over the pretraining data. More importantly, we combine these lines of research, studying both generalizing mechanisms and token overlap, and how they develop and interact over time.

3 Model Pretraining

To form the basis of our study, we pretrain a LLaMA-style causal decoder-only language model Touvron et al. (2023) with 1.71.7B parameters from scratch on nine languages: English, French, German, Indonesian, Italian, Portuguese, Spanish, Mandarin Chinese, and Japanese, covering three different script families. English training data is drawn from FineWeb-HQ Messmer et al. (2025a), the remaining languages from FineWeb2-HQ Messmer et al. (2025b). Each batch consists of a multilingual mixture of sequences sampled according to probabilities of 0.5 for English, and 0.0625 for each of the remaining languages. We capture model checkpoints at a granularity of 185185M tokens, providing 200200 snapshots across training for our fine-grained analysis. We report full model training details in Appendix A.

4 Evaluation

We use two main tasks to track the development of our model’s monolingual and cross-lingual ability.

4.1 Linguistic Acceptability

The first task focuses on evaluating linguistic capabilities by evaluation on BLiMP-style minimal pairs. For English, German, French, Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese, we use the respective subsets of MultiBLiMP Jumelet et al. (2025). Japanese, Chinese, and Indonesian are not included in MultiBLiMP; we use JBLiMP Someya and Oseki (2023), ZhoBLiMP Liu et al. (2024) and the Indonesian subset of LINDSEA BLiMP (Leong et al., 2023, hereafter referred to as LINDSEA), respectively. Since ZhoBLiMP is significantly bigger than the other datasets, we randomly subsample 30 examples for each phenomenon, matching the larger MultiBLiMP partitions in size. We use the LM Evaluation Harness Gao et al. (2024) to compute the length-normalized variant of accuracy.

4.2 Word-Level Translation Data

The second task is word-level translation (WLT), taken to study cross-lingual transfer. Prior interpretability studies of cross-lingual generalizing mechanisms have largely focused on frequently-used, simple nouns, partly due to methodological constraints such as reliance on unique first tokens Wendler et al. (2024); Dumas et al. (2025). Since we aim to study natural language use, we construct a novel dataset, balanced across word class and frequency ranks, and allowing for inflection. To do so, we curate language-pair specific valid translations for each source word, allowing polysemous words and words that belong to multiple word classes, e.g., “dance” may be translated to both the verb “tanzen” and the noun “Tanz” in German.

Our concepts are drawn from ChiKhaPo, a multilingual lexical benchmark Chang and Bafna (2025). We use ‘‘concept’’ to describe an abstract idea that can be expressed by different words. We randomly select 125 concepts, balanced across English frequency (as determined by fastText,​33 3 cc.en.300.bin Grave et al., 2018); we discard any word that is not in the top 20k most frequent. Additionally, we ensure coverage of English word classes (as determined by WordNet44 4 https://wordnet.princeton.edu/ via NLTK, Bird, 2006), selecting 40 nouns, 40 verbs, 25 adjectives, and 20 adverbs.

We split the concepts into 25 few-shot and 100 query examples. Importantly, in the query set, we allow for identical cognates, such as “ala” (meaning “wing” in both Spanish and Italian) to reflect natural language use—these make up 4.4%4.4\% of word pairs across all language pairs. However, we require that few-shot examples are unique across languages to prime the model to translate instead of copy. Given this constraint, we secondarily maintain coverage of PoS and frequency bins in the few-shot set on a best-effort basis.

The resulting multi-way parallel dataset includes 125 concepts aligned across our nine languages, with language-pair specific valid translations for the 100 query concepts. We detail our dataset construction process in Appendix B.

4.3 Prompt Construction

We follow Wendler et al. (2024) for prompt construction. Given ℓs​r​c/ℓt​g​t\ell_{src}/\ell_{tgt} as the source and target language and ws​r​c/wt​g​tw_{src}/w_{tgt} as the source and target word for the same concept, each prompt consists of five examples, formulated as ℓi​n\ell_{in}: “ws​r​cw_{src}” - ℓt​g​t\ell_{tgt}: “wt​g​tw_{tgt}”, followed by a query, ending in ℓi​n\ell_{in}: ws​r​cw_{src} - ℓt​g​t\ell_{tgt}: “. For example, for the source word “dance”:

ℓs​r​c/ℓt​g​t\ell_{src}/\ell_{tgt} are expressed in their own language, in this case Deutsch for ℓt​g​t\ell_{tgt} German. We also evaluate a variant of this task, referred to as repetition, where source and target language are equivalent and the word simply has to be copied.

We measure case-insensitive mean accuracy, counting a word as correctly translated if it matches one of the synonyms. For the repetition task, we count a word as correctly repeated if it matches the source word (see Appendix C for further details).

5 Model Learning Phases

WLT accuracy improves gradually during training, reaching a final mean accuracy of 32.1%32.1\% (Fig. 2(a)). Error analysis shows that copying is the dominant error mode, peaking at 53.2%53.2\% of errors attributable to erroneous copying across all language pairs (Fig. 1, see Appendix C for detailed analysis). We also observe cases where token overlap misleads the model. For example, when asked to translate “irrtümlich” (mistaken) from German to French, the model outputs “irréparable” (irreparable) instead of “erroné”, copying the initial token, “irr”, and continuing in the target language with the wrong meaning.

However, copying can also be a useful strategy: token overlap can aid translation, and in some cases, copying is the correct strategy. For example, “incorrectamente” (meaning: incorrectly) is a valid translation from Spanish to Portuguese. We refer to this as valid copying; our WLT dataset includes 4.4%4.4\% such instances. As Fig. 1 shows, word pairs with partial overlap are learned earlier and more quickly, in line with Kallini et al. (2025).

The model must therefore learn not only how to copy, but also when. In parallel, it must learn to translate without token overlap, and when to prefer translation over copying. We identify two phases characterizing this learning process.

Phase I – Development of Copy Mechanism

In Phase I, we observe a rapid increase in performance on both the repetition task (Fig. 2(b)) and MultiBLiMP (Fig. 2(c)). By 9.59.5B processed tokens, the model reaches 94.1%94.1\% average accuracy on the repetition task and surpasses 90%90\% for each MultiBLiMP subset. In parallel, the loss shows a steep decline (see Appendix Fig. 7), generalizing Chen et al. (2025)’s similar findings in an English-only encoder model to the multilingual setting.

In WLT, copying is increasingly the dominant error mode, plateauing between 7−157-15B tokens processed at up to 56.3%56.3\% of model outputs. We observe two main variants of copying: context copying, where the model copies one of the few-shot examples, and source word copying, where the model copies the source word. We consider context copying a less targeted variant, with source word copying indicating that the model has learned to attend to the right part of the prompt.

During Phase I, copying becomes more targeted. As shown in Fig. 1, the rate of context copying rises to 33.6%33.6\% of outputs until 6.76.7B tokens processed, and then falls for the rest of training. The rate of source word copying begins to rise later, overtaking context copying after 7.57.5B tokens. A similar pattern appears in the repetition task, where context copying is even more prevalent, but also decays more quickly over training (see Appendix Fig. 11).

Performance on ZhoBLiMP, JBLiMP, and LINDSEA is notably lower than on MultiBLiMP. However, our model’s performance matches the top scores reported by the respective authors (83%83\%, Liu et al., 2024, 78%78\%, Someya and Oseki, 2023, and 22%−65%22\%-65\% Leong et al., 2023).

Phase II – Transition to Translation

At around 1111B tokens processed, we observe the first successful predictions in WLT for word pairs without token overlap (Fig. 1), indicating the development of generalizing mechanisms. Meanwhile, erroneous copying begins a steady decline that continues for the rest of training, suggesting the model’s diminishing reliance on copying.

6 Interpretability Methods

To understand how token-level copying and translation develop and interact over our model’s learning phases we study the training dynamics of its internal components. We apply two complementary interpretability methods: logit lens Nostalgebraist (2020) to track how prediction candidates compete over layers, and ExPLAIND Eichin et al. (2025) to identify what model components and data drive these predictions.

6.1 Logit Lens: Layer-Wise Analysis

We use logit lens Nostalgebraist (2020) to analyze the representation of concepts in our nine languages at different layers and checkpoints. This method projects intermediate hidden states into the vocabulary space by passing the last token’s activation from each layer through the model’s final normalization, unembedding, and log softmax. For multi-token words, we utilize teacher forcing: we sequentially append the ground-truth tokens of a candidate word to the context and extract the intermediate log probability for each successive token. We normalize the sum of these log probabilities by length to compare candidates.

Multilingual Analysis

To apply logit lens to a concept (Section 4.2) while accounting for its lexical variation, we evaluate all its synonyms and use the one with the highest score at the final layer. Although a prompt specifies a single target translation direction (e.g., English to German), we repeat the process to extract the concept’s score across all nine languages. This lets us track layer-wise scores for a concept across the model and compare relative language-(in)dependent trends.

Copy vs. Translate Analysis

To analyze how target (translation) and source (copy) candidates compete over layers, we define the translation-over-copy margin:

mL=log⁡pL​(wtgt)−log⁡pL​(wsrc).m_{L}=\log p_{L}(w_{\text{tgt}})-\log p_{L}(w_{\text{src}}).

where wtgtw_{\text{tgt}} is the translation candidate, wsrcw_{\text{src}} the copy candidate and log⁡pL​(w)\log p_{L}(w) the (normalized) log probability of a word at layer LL, as well as its layer-wise difference Δ​mL→L+1=mL+1−mL\Delta m_{L\to L+1}=m_{L+1}-m_{L}. A negative Δ​mL→L+1\Delta m_{L\to L+1} indicates a layer transition where the source word is preferred over the target word—we refer to such transitions as copy promoting. Conversely, a positive Δ​mL→L+1\Delta m_{L\to L+1} indicates that the transition is translation promoting.

6.2 ExPLAIND: Attribution over Model Components and Data

We use the ExPLAIND framework Eichin et al. (2025) to identify relevant model parameters and quantify the influence of different types of training data on our two mechanisms. The framework decomposes the loss trajectory L⁡(θs,x)L(\theta_{s},x) of an unseen sample xx onto the model parameters θt\theta_{t} at step ss and training samples xkx_{k} , computing influence scores ϕ⁡(s,θs(i),xk,x)∈ℝ\phi(s,\theta_{s}^{(i)},x_{k},x)\in\mathbb{R} which add up to L⁡(θs,x)L(\theta_{s},x).

We subsample the training steps ss to every 500th step, i.e., each one of our checkpoints. Furthermore, since we are interested in global rather than local influences, we accumulate influence scores over collections of samples for both the predictions and training data and over parameters to the layer level (following Eichin et al., 2025). Thus, for a step ss the influence through parameters Θs\Theta_{s} of a training data partition XX onto a set of predictions BB is:

Ψ⁡(s,Θs,X,B)=∑x^∈B∑x∈X∑θ∈Θsϕ⁡(s,θ,x,x^).\Psi(s,\Theta_{s},X,B)=\sum_{\hat{x}\in B}\sum_{x\in X}\sum_{\theta\in\Theta_{s}}\phi(s,\theta,x,\hat{x}).

Negative influences imply a decrease in loss, i.e., the model is more likely to make the prediction xx.

To isolate the parameters involved in competition between copy and translate we study the influence of simulated training data on erroneously copied and successfully translated predictions. We hypothesize that parallel data as well as the target word occurrences encourage translation. We construct such data Xp​a​r​a​l​l​e​lX_{parallel} (see Section D.3) and combine it with the training batches of our checkpoints to simulate training data.

We sample a set of erroneously copied predictions (Bc​o​p​yB_{copy}), and corresponding correctly translated predictions (Bt​r​a​n​s​l​a​t​eB_{translate}). Sets are aligned across source words: for each ws​r​cw_{src}, Bc​o​p​yB_{copy} includes ws​r​c→ws​r​cw_{src}\rightarrow w_{src}, and Bt​r​a​n​s​l​a​t​eB_{translate} includes ws​r​c→wt​g​tw_{src}\rightarrow w_{tgt} (see Section D.2). We define

Dc​o​p​y​(s,Θ):=Ψ⁡(s,Θ,Xp​a​r​a​l​l​e​l,Bc​o​p​y)−Ψ⁡(s,Θ,Xp​a​r​a​l​l​e​l,Bt​r​a​n​s​l​a​t​e).\begin{split}D_{copy}(s,\Theta):=&\Psi(s,\Theta,X_{parallel},B_{copy})\\ &-\Psi(s,\Theta,X_{parallel},B_{translate}).\end{split}

and consider the most negative parameter groups in terms of Dc​o​p​yD_{copy} during Phase I as copy promoting, and the most positive in terms of Dc​o​p​yD_{copy} in Phase II as copy suppressing. We rank parameters by the corresponding influences and only keep the ones with at least 50%50\% of the TOP-1’s influence. For comparison, we also study the layer-wise influence of the actual training data Xt​r​a​i​nX_{train} on a sample of WLT predictions BWLTB_{\textsc{WLT}}.

7 Model Component Analysis

7.1 Copy Mechanism

The logit lens margin plot identifies several copy-promoting layer transitions 7→87\to 8, 12→1312\to 13, and more weakly 15→1715\to 17 (Fig. 3(a)). Throughout Phase II, the layer-wise dynamics of copying change little; the copy-promoting layer transitions established during Phase I persist. However, the target candidate rises steadily while the source candidate is progressively down-ranked in Phase II, indicating an increased preference for translation (Fig. 3(b)). Notably, we also observe upper layers down-ranking valid translation candidates with partial or even full token overlap with the source word (see Appendix Fig. 13), suggesting a mechanism that discourages token copying for translation, even though the model ultimately prefers such outputs. While logit lens offers insights into the preferred prediction at a particular layer, it does not reveal which components influence these. To understand how parameters in the model drive the observed changes, we turn to ExPLAIND.

We use ExPLAIND to identify the most copy-promoting parameters in Phase I, and the most copy-suppressing parameters in Phase II (Section 6.2). We probe their role by performing two ablations. First, we scale them by 2.02.0 to excite their influence on the predictions. Second, we scale by 0.50.5 to inhibit their influence. We compare the ablated checkpoint’s copy and translation behavior to that of the original checkpoint.

ExPLAIND identifies the attention value projections in layers 0−20-2 as the TOP-3 contributors of copy-promoting influence in Phase I (see Fig. 4(b)). We find that exciting their influence makes copy behavior dominant throughout training (both source word and context copying is almost tripled in the final checkpoint), while halving it inhibits copying with only minor impact on translation performance (less than 44 percentage points), primarily affecting instances where token copying produces correct translations (see Section F.2). This indicates that parameters in layers 0−20-2 control whether to copy.

ExPLAIND identifies parameters in layers 6−96-9 (listed in Section D.4) as the top contributors of copy-suppressing influence in Phase II. We find that exciting them results in both higher context copying and higher source word copying (tripled and doubled in the ablated final checkpoint, respectively). Inhibiting them results in even higher context copying, but does not have this same effect on source word copying (quadrupled in the ablated final checkpoint). By contrast, the unablated model has learned to copy specifically the source word by this point (albeit incorrectly). This suggests a more complicated role of the parameters in layers 6−96-9: they are calibrated to control where to copy from, as inhibiting them causes untargeted copying, but also, whether to copy, as exciting them results in both targeted and untargeted copying.

Taken together, the parameters in these lower layers drive much of the copy decision. We hypothesize that this, in combination with the increasing translation signal seen in the logit lens margin plot (Fig. 3(a)), leads to improved translation. Further, that the increased translation signal reflects the development of a generalizing mechanism, which we investigate in the following section.

7.2 Transition to Translation

Prior work casts multilingual processing as a hierarchical, three-stage process: first, the bottom layers map from the input language to an intermediate shared space, in which inputs are processed, and third, the top layers map to the output language Zhao et al. (2024). Our logit lens analysis of the final checkpoint supports this—candidates across languages only separate in the top block (Fig. 5). However, it does not reveal how the generalizing mechanisms implementing shared spaces develop over training, or how their emergence relates to the transition to translation.

We test this through targeted layer swapping experiments. We group the model’s layers into bottom, intermediate, and top blocks, based on observable model behavior. The bottom block includes the copy-promoting layers (Section 7.1), and the upper block begins where the logit lens shows other language candidates are downranked relative to the source and target. This results in blocks of 00–99, 1010–1515, and 1616–2323, respectively (indicated in Fig. 5). Importantly, we combine static blocks from different points in training (as proposed by Bandarkar et al., 2024). Combining a final checkpoint’s blocks with the respective blocks of earlier checkpoints and evaluating the resulting models’ accuracy gives an indication of the development of each block.

Emergence of Generalizing Mechanisms

To isolate the contribution of the intermediate block as it develops, we swap bottom+top blocks of the final checkpoint into earlier checkpoints and observe WLT accuracy. The results in Fig. 6 show a striking pattern: over all checkpoints after 1010B tokens processed, the swapped model shows an improvement of up to 30%30\% of the final performance relative to the original model. After a steep increase following the transition to Phase II, the curve flattens, reaching 90%90\% of the final performance at roughly the midway point (18.818.8B tokens processed), and 98%98\% by 2525B tokens processed. This indicates that the generalizing mechanisms in the intermediate layers are largely formed between 44B and 18.818.8B tokens, with smaller refinements until 2525B. By then, subsequent changes in the intermediate layers do not further improve performance. Learning gains in the second half of Phase II thus stem not from development of generalizing intermediate layers, but rather improvements in the bottom+top blocks.

Reduced Reliance on Copying

We further find that other combinations of swapped layers lead to increased WLT performance. Notably, the WLT performance when swapping in the final checkpoint’s bottom and intermediate blocks is on par with the bottom + top block setting in the first half of training (Fig. 6). We hypothesize that this is not just due to the generalizing mechanisms in the intermediate block, but also refined copy initiation and routing in the bottom block (Section 7.1). We confirm this by observing the ablated models’ copying behavior (dotted lines in Fig. 6). Checkpoints paired with the final bottom+intermediate blocks do not show the peaks in copy errors at the transition from Phase I to II, suggesting that the two blocks combined implement most of the decision mechanisms to promote translation and reduce copying. In contrast, the bottom+top block setting does not exhibit this reduction in copy behavior, but rather promotes it in the first half of training.

Taken together, these ablations support the role of the intermediate block in cross-lingual generalization, as identified by prior work Bandarkar and Peng (2025). However, it also suggests that the bottom block in combination with the intermediate block is needed to suppress erroneous copy behavior. This connects back to the ablations in Section 7.1, which identify layer groups 00–22 and 66–99 as refining the model’s copy behavior.

8 Discussion

We study the development of two mechanisms that appear central to word-level translation: token-level copying Feucht et al. (2025), and translation via shared concept spaces Wendler et al. (2024), identifying two learning phases that characterize the evolution and interplay of these mechanisms: Phase I, in which token-level copying is learned, Phase II, in which generalizing mechanisms develop and copying is deprioritized (Section 5).

We find that the copying mechanism is a strong early strategy, developing in parallel with basic linguistic capabilities. The copy-promoting mechanism established in Phase I persists throughout training, becoming more targeted. It is increasingly deprioritized as the model develops translation capabilities—the model’s reduced reliance on copying coincides with the development of generalizing mechanisms. Later training gains from the lower layers of the model reflect refinement of the copy mechanism throughout training as the model copies more selectively (Section 7.1).

Surprisingly, the generalizing mechanisms enabling translation develop by the halfway point of our pretraining. Through our layer-swapping experiments, we discover that the intermediate layers alone enable translation, but the bottom and intermediate layers together are needed to deprioritize erroneous copying (Section 7.2).

A natural question is what drives the development of these generalizing mechanisms. As a first probe, we ask whether simple distributional features of our pretraining data predict when a word is first correctly translated: source and target word frequency, and their co-occurrence. However, these features collectively explain less than 9%9\% of the variance, suggesting that surface statistics are poor proxies for the underlying translation signal (see Appendix E for details). We hypothesize that incidental parallel data play a more important role Briakou et al. (2023), as supported by the simulated parallel data studied through ExPLAIND (Fig. 4(b)), but leave systematic investigation to future work.

9 Conclusion

We study incidental cross-lingual transfer, using the task of word-level translation as a testbed. We argue that studying the final model alone does not allow for insights into how the underlying mechanisms develop and interact. To this end, we pretrain a multilingual 1.71.7B model on nine diverse languages. We identify two learning phases that are characterized by the development of two central mechanisms: token-level copying, and generalizing mechanisms that implement shared spaces, enabling translation. Using complementary interpretability approaches to analyze how these mechanisms emerge and interact, we find that token-level copying is a strong early strategy, learned in parallel with basic linguistic capabilities. As training progresses, the generalizing mechanism increasingly enables translation, coinciding with a decline in copying as an error mode. Together, these findings shed light on how incidental word-level translation develops in multilingual language models.

Limitations

Our WLT benchmark is designed as a controlled testbed for cross-lingual transfer, though it captures only one part of the broader phenomenon and leaves open how these dynamics extend to words in context and reasoning-heavy tasks. Its evaluation depends on curated synonym sets for each concept, which are not exhaustive and may miss valid translations which can underestimate translation accuracy and bias comparisons toward better-covered languages.

Although our studied model (1.71.7B parameters) is sufficiently large to exhibit non-trivial multilingual behavior, our analysis is restricted to this setting. The training run has not converged, so our conclusions concern the dynamics observed during early pretraining and may not fully extend to fully-trained multilingual models.

We further acknowledge specific technical limitations associated with the methods used for our component-level analysis. For logit lens, teacher forcing introduces a length- and tokenization-dependent bias: multi-token words are scored via multiple conditioned steps, even with length-normalization. In addition, absolute logit-lens scores are affected by script-dependent biases in the output embedding. Another known limitation of the logit lens is that intermediate residual-stream states are not necessarily calibrated to be compatible by the final unembedding. We also note that while ExPLAIND offers novel perspectives from which to study model behavior, its explanations do not inform about the causal effect that changes in the model or data would have on the model behavior. We address some of these objections by performing different model interventions with layer swapping and activation scaling over time. While they support our hypotheses, we do not perform them exhaustively over all possible settings due to their computational cost. This might occlude other interesting dynamics.

In our layer-swapping experiments, we group layers into bottom, intermediate, and top blocks to parallel existing literature Zhao et al. (2024), despite our logit lens analysis suggesting them to be less distinct than in previous work. We hypothesize that this apparent two-stage process is inherent to translation, which simply maps representations into and out of a shared space, whereas tasks demanding complex cross-lingual reasoning (e.g., math problems) might exhibit more pronounced intermediate processing. Indeed, our layer-swapping experiments suggest that the bottom and intermediate blocks develop concurrently rather than sequentially. Furthermore, we note that no single correct boundary exists, as optimal splits vary with the task at hand Bandarkar and Peng (2025). In addition, while we argue for the emergence of shared representational spaces, our methodology does not directly examine the underlying activations (cf. Dumas et al. (2025)). However, our layer-swapping experiments still provide convincing evidence for their existence.

Ethical Considerations

This paper presents work aimed to advance the fundamental understanding of multilingual pretraining. While the development of general AI capabilities carries broad societal implications, we do not believe our specific findings necessitate individual highlighting in this respect. Our work focuses on interpretability, which contributes to the broader goal of algorithmic transparency. However, there is an inherent ethical risk of over-reliance on such insights. Despite these risks, the goal of improving cross-lingual transfer is a significant positive consequence. Through a better understanding of cross-lingual transfer, our work can inform future work on the inclusion of low-resource languages in global AI development and help bridge the digital divide.

We disclose that AI tools were used during this research for support with code generation, ideation, writing and experimental suggestions. To ensure the integrity of the work, all AI-generated outputs were rigorously verified by the authors, and we confirm that we take full responsibility for the final content and results presented.

Appendix A Additional Details on Pretraining

The model is a decoder-only transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) following the LLaMA architecture (Touvron et al., 2023), with 24 decoder layers, a hidden size of 2048, and standard LLaMA components such as multi-head attention, RMSNorm and rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) with a high base. We provide an overview of all parameters of the model in Table 1.

We use the Tekken (Mistral–Nemo) tokenizer (Mistral AI, 2024), a state-of-the-art multilingual tokenizer (Apertus et al., 2025) that provides broad script coverage.

We train the model using the widely adopted AdamW optimizer (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) with a peak learning rate of 1×10−41\times 10^{-4}. The learning rate schedule follows a wst-decay scheme Hu et al. (2024), which first increases the learning rate linearly, plateaus for most of the training, and then decreases proportionally to 1/t1/\sqrt{t}. We apply gradient clipping at 1.0 for stability under mixed-precision training. These settings follow established practice Martins et al. (2025). We report the exact parameters in Table 1.

We draw our pretraining data from the FineWeb2-HQ and FineWeb-HQ datasets (Messmer et al., 2025a; Messmer et al., 2025b). The mixture covers nine languages spanning multiple scripts (Latin, Han, and Japanese). Sampling probabilities are listed in Table 1, with English accounting for 50%50\% of all samples and the remaining eight languages drawn uniformly. We do not exhaust any of the monolingual datasets during training and every data point is seen at most once.

We implement the training in Python using PyTorch. The model implementation uses the LlamaForCausalLM module from the HuggingFace transformers library.55 5 https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/model_doc/llama Distributed training across eight NVIDIA A100 GPUs is handled via the accelerate library from HuggingFace. In total, the run processes approximately 3737B tokens and converges to a final training loss of 2.582.58, consistent with expectations for models of comparable scale and architecture (Allal et al., 2025). Pretraining was completed in 281.4281.4 hours.

We summarize the model architecture, optimizer settings, and training configuration in Table 1, as well as the loss curve in Fig. 7.

Appendix B Word-Level Translation Dataset Construction

Here we provide additional details on the construction of the word-level translation (WLT) dataset, which comprises 100 target words in nine languages with valid translations for all 72 directed language pairs accounting for polysemy. In this study, we focus on natural language use. To this end, we allow for inflection and words that belong to multiple word classes, which may otherwise be excluded from WLT tasks to avoid ambiguity in the target translation. When stratifying over word classes, we use a simple heuristic to assign a primary PoS tag, first querying WordNet66 6 https://wordnet.princeton.edu/ via NLTK, Bird, 2006 for each word’s attested syntactic categories. A word was considered a member of a PoS class if WordNet contained at least one synset for that word under the corresponding category (noun, verb, adjective, or adverb; adjective satellites were merged with adjectives). When a word belonged to multiple categories, we applied a priority ordering of noun > verb > adjective > adverb. An additional rule handled gerunds (ending in “-ing”): if the stem had verbal synsets, these were assigned the verb class. We override the heuristic only once, for “complex”, where it assigned “adjective”, an unintuitive label. We show the final distribution over PoS tag sets in Table 2, and curate a set of valid translations to reflect this PoS tag ambiguity.

As described in Section 4.2, constructing a set of valid translations for WLT requires careful consideration. We source our concepts from ChiKhaPo Chang and Bafna (2025), but find that the synsets are in some cases too broad for our purposes, including words that would only be considered a valid translation in very specific contexts. In other cases, they are not broad enough, for example not including gendered variants. Therefore, we come up with a multi-source voting procedure to filter and introduce candidates. For each source word, language-pair specific candidate translations were collected from four evidence streams:

  • •

    Machine translation outputs given the source word from multiple MT systems: Aya-Expanse-32B Dang et al. (2024), translategemma-27b-it Google Translate Research Team et al. (2026), madlad400-10b-mt Kudugunta et al. (2023), mbart-large-50-many-to-many-mmt Tang et al. (2020), and nllb-200-3.3B Team et al. (2022)).

  • •

    Lexicon entries: ChiKhaPo for non-English targets and Merriam-Webster77 7 https://www.merriam-webster.com/ synonyms and thesaurus entries for English targets.

  • •

    DeepL88 8 https://www.deepl.com/ translations of the source word, and DeepL sense-based translations of the English word (using Merriam-Webster entries), filtered by back-translation match.

  • •

    Back-translation verification, where candidates translating back to the source word received an additional vote.

Candidates were required to be supported by at least one MT system; lexicon-only candidates (ChiKhaPo, Merriam-Webster) contributed fractional votes but could not admit a candidate alone. The candidate sets were subsequently filtered using an LLM judge (claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929). For each source word and every target language (72 language pairs total), the model was prompted to discard candidates with mismatching part of speech, number, or meaning, while retaining morphological variants (e.g. gendered forms) when the source word is under-specified. We show the system prompt in Fig. 8, and refer readers to our research code for full details. We verify that the LLM does not introduce new words, mitigating the risk of hallucinations. Finally, we manually check the resulting candidates.

We acknowledge that this pipeline is an approximation of gold human judgment. We expect errors to be predominantly false negatives, i.e., valid translations excluded by conservative filtering, which would lead to slight underestimates of model accuracy rather than inflated scores.

We verify that the benchmark is tractable by evaluating EuroLLM 1.71.7B Martins et al. (2025), a similarly sized multilingual model, which achieves an accuracy of 61.1%61.1\%. This is notably higher than our final model’s performance, which we attribute to the difference in pretraining data size: EuroLLM 1.71.7B is trained on 44T tokens, compared to our 3737B.

Appendix C Additional Details on Word-Level Translation Evaluation

C.1 Experimental Setup

We greedily decode model outputs, allowing up to 16 tokens (corresponding to the longest valid translation in our WLT dataset). If a ” is found, we split on this, otherwise, we use the full decoded output. A word is counted as correctly translated if its lowercased form matches one of the lowercased valid translations. For the repetition task, a word is counted as correctly repeated if its lowercased form matches the lowercased source word.

We count a word as a source word copying if the lowercased generated word matches the lowercased source word. Source-word copying can be valid, as is the case for the word “ala” (wing in both Spanish and Italian). We count an output as context copying, when it matches the target word of any of the few-shot examples in the prompt, modulo casing.

C.2 Evaluation

We complement the metrics reported in Figs. 1 and 2, with additional statistics about WLT performance, alongside further noteworthy observations from our analysis.

Translation accuracy

Fig. 9(a) presents the final translation accuracy for each directed language pair. Surprisingly, accuracy is not monotonic. Out of 7,2007,200 word pairs, 57.8%57.8\% are predicted correctly at some point in training, but are often not consistently correct after this point. We further observe a pronounced directional asymmetry in performance; for instance, the accuracy of translating to English is significantly higher than translating from English, as evidenced by the distinct dark column in the heatmap. We hypothesize that this is due to English’s role as the dominant language during pretraining. To a lesser extent, accuracy into Japanese and Chinese also exceeds the accuracy of translating from those languages, a phenomenon potentially reflecting higher language extractability afforded by their unique scripts. As shown in Fig. 9(b), this directional asymmetry emerges early, coinciding with the start of Phase II, and continues to develop throughout the remainder of pretraining. Notably, the asymmetry for English reaches a plateau mid-way through this phase, indicating that reciprocal directions are being learned at a similar rate, while the asymmetry for other language pairs continues to widen.

Copying as an error mode

Fig. 11 shows the decomposition of model outputs into specific error modes throughout training. Context copying is a frequent error also for the repetition task, exceeding the respective rate on the word-level-translation task, but decaying faster. We further observe that copying behavior is highly language-dependent. The fraction of incorrect translations attributable to source word copying varies significantly across pairs (Fig. 10). This suggests that a script difference discourages source word copying. At the end of training, this error mode is especially present for language pairs with the highest frequency of valid copies in the WLT data, namely Spanish↔\leftrightarrowPortuguese (50%/49%50\%/49\%), as well as Japanese↔\leftrightarrowChinese (27%/20%27\%/20\%).

Role of token overlap

We categorize each data sample into one of three buckets based on their token overlap: Of the 7,2007,200 word pairs, 4.40%4.40\% are valid copies, 18.5%18.5\% have partial token overlap, and the majority, 77.1%77.1\%, have no token overlap. In general, and in line with previous literature Kallini et al. (2025), we find that token overlap aids translation, with a higher accuracy on these pairs. As shown in Fig. 12(c), the model achieves roughly 90%90\% accuracy on valid copies, with a slight dip in accuracy in early Phase II. This matches our analysis which shows that during this transition, the model suppresses copying. Differentiating the copying variants with respect to token overlap (Figs. 12(a) and 12(b)), we observe that partial token overlap increases erroneous source word copying, whereas context copying is more prevalent for words with no token overlap. This suggests token overlap supports source word copying as a more targeted copying.

Appendix D Additional Details on ExPLAIND Experiment Settings and Methodology

D.1 Mathematical Details on ExPLAIND

We refer the interested reader to Eichin et al. (2025) for details on the methodology and theoretical considerations regarding ExPLAIND. Since we train our model using AdamW Loshchilov and Hutter (2019), we can directly use their formulation.

Since computing the full ExPLAIND decomposition is infeasible for large models and data, we rely on Eichin et al. (2025)’s efficient implementation and consider only every 500th parameter update, as well as a subsample of 20%20\% of the training data for all experiments besides the accuracy sanity check below.

Accuracy of the ExPLAIND decomposition.

We investigate whether the decomposition of the actual training influences through ExPLAIND actually recovers the loss trajectory. I.e., whether summing up all the scores is equal to the actual difference of losses in the respective step. We find that this is indeed the case: Over a subsample (N=200 WLT predictions) of the data, the average difference of the sum of scores to the actual loss change is less than 1%1\% with a standard deviation of one percentage point over a sample of 50 checkpoints uniformly sampled from the ones available to us.

Influence of first moment term.

Since we only track a subsample of the checkpoints, tracking the indirect influence of data from previous update steps through the first moment term is only possible for scores, where we accumulate over the data dimension of the tensor of influences. I.e., we cannot track the influence of single instances or partitions, only the overall influence. This is because, while we have the summed up first moment term from the optimizer checkpoints, disentangling it to the level of previously seen data requires processing these steps and keeping terms for each sample. As Eichin et al. (2025) argue, this is infeasible for large models like ours. In the current study, we present two experiments using ExPLAIND: (1) Influence of the actual training data (shown in Fig. 4), where we accumulate over the data dimension. Here, we include the influences from the first moment terms; (2) the influence of simulated parallel samples (shown in Fig. 4(b)), where we cannot quantify the influence of the first moment.

D.2 Test Partitions for ExPLAIND Analysis

We study different aspects of our model behavior through the loss decomposition of data batches that exhibit the respective behavior. The details on these test partitions (a naming we adopt from Eichin et al. (2025)’s terminology to mean is part of the test set or the (unseen) samples we want to explain) are presented in the following.

WLT instances BW​L​TB_{WLT}.

We sample a set of WLT instances from the pool of concepts that are predicted correctly for at least half of the translations. Since computational complexity of the decomposition is high, we restrict ourselves to instances where the source and target language are Chinese, German, French, or English. The loss we decompose for these instances is computed solely based on the tokens that constitute the target word in the sequences, the rest of the tokens are masked. This way, we isolate the prediction of the WLT target from other factors such as predicting quotations etc.

Challenging WLT instances Bt​r​a​n​s​l​a​t​eB_{translate}.

From the complementary set of WLT concepts which were predicted correctly for less than half of the translations, we sample a set of “challenging” WLT instances. We again focus on the same languages. Furthermore, we verify that copying is the majority error mode in this set during the Phase I, where copying is dominant.

Copy WLT instances Bc​o​p​yB_{copy}.

To decompose copy behavior, we take the challenging WLT instances and switch their correct WLT target with the source word. In other words, we create samples where copy is assumed to be the "correct" behavior in the loss function we decompose. This loss increases for instances where non-copy behavior becomes the model’s preferred strategy. In other words, by decomposing and contrasting the copy instances with the correct behavior, we can isolate the parts of the model that promote and suppress this behavior over time.

D.3 Training Partitions for ExPLAIND Analysis

As we describe in Section 6.2, ExPLAIND can be leveraged to study the parameter-wise influence of a training data partition onto the predictions over time. In this work, we rely on two main sources for training data partitions to study our model’s training dynamics. Namely:

Actual training data Xt​r​a​i​nX_{train}.

For the checkpoints we consider, we store the complete training batch that was used to update the parameters to the next checkpoint. In other words, we store the (unseen) data that is used to compute the next training gradients. Since we are interested in cross-language influences, we partition this data by the language distribution it came from, i.e. the language of the FineWeb-HQ subset the data was taken from. This leads to nine training data partitions, one for each language we include.

Parallel data Xp​a​r​a​l​l​e​lX_{parallel}.

To investigate the mechanisms behind copying, we introduce another training partition, which consists of parallel data, which we describe in the following. We assume that this type of data would introduce learning influences that support beneficial WLT behavior Kondo et al. (2024) and suppress copying as a fallback, especially on instances that are not predicted correctly.

First, two annotators from the team of authors, of which one is an English native speaker and the other has a C1 level IELTS certificate, were instructed to write short, simple sentences that use each of the concepts in English. The annotators checked each other’s sentences to avoid incorrect or disfluent samples.

We then proceeded to use an ensemble of machine translation models to generate translations of the sentences in the remaining eight languages, namely nllb-200-3.3B Team et al. (2022) and translategemma-27B-it Google Translate Research Team et al. (2026), which support all of our language pairs, and the language-pair specific models from the opus-mt family of models Tiedemann and Thottingal (2020). To get a rough proxy for translation quality, for each translation, we backtranslate using the same model and measure the cosine similarity of sequence embeddings produced by Qwen3-Embedding-4B Zhang et al. (2025) of the original and the backtranslated sentence. For each sample and language, we keep the highest scoring translation in terms of that cosine similarity.

To simulate the appearance of simple parallel data without much interference from other factors, we concatenate the resulting translations back-to-back, separating them by a single whitespace. Our WLT test partition is restricted to German, French, English, and Chinese. Accordingly, we only consider the respective parallel training data for these languages. For the other languages, the translations are nevertheless included in the supplements of this work. Note that this training data is simulated, in the sense that it was not actually part of the training batch at this checkpoint. ExPLAIND allows for this by simply adding these simulated samples to the actual training batch and computing the decomposition in the same manner.

D.4 Identifying Copy Parameters using ExPLAIND

To identify the parameter groups most relevant to copying, we rank them according to their negative ExPLAIND influence in Phase I and their positive influence in Phase II. To keep our interventions sparse, we choose the affected groups by including only the ones which have at least half of the maximum influence.

In Phase I, this identifies attention value projects of layers 1−31-3 as the most relevant to copy learning in that phase.

In Phase II, we identify the attention key and query projections in layer 9, the attention key and value projection in layer 8, and the MLP down projections of layer 6 and 7 as the most relevant layers.

Appendix E Data Distribution Analysis

How well does training data distribution predict translation learning?

To understand how the distribution of our data influences the trajectory of word-pair learning, we use WIMBD Elazar et al. (2024) to collect cumulative frequency counts of source words, valid translations, and their co-occurrence across training steps. We define co-occurrence as both words appearing within 150 characters of each other in a sequence, using word boundaries for Latin-script languages.

Since these features are inherently correlated (Pearson correlation between 0.31−0.460.31-0.46), we perform a Shapley value decomposition of R2R^{2} Azen and Budescu (2003) to analyze their relative importance in predicting when a word pair is first correctly translated, excluding those that are never correctly translated. We also exclude word pairs where a copy is possible, i.e., any of the valid translations exactly matches the source word. Since our synonym lists vary in length, and are not guaranteed to cover all synonyms, we choose the most frequent count and co-occurrence count across the set of valid translations for our predictors.

The three predictors explain only 8.7%8.7\% of the variance in when a word pair is first translated correctly. Of the explained variance, source word frequency accounts for 45.1%45.1\%, co-occurrence for 37.3%37.3\%, and target word frequency for 17.6%17.6\%. Overall, this indicates that simple corpus frequency statistics alone are not a strong predictor of when a word is successfully translated. We leave further investigation to future work.

We include additional results of our analysis that were omitted from the main paper for brevity.

F.1 Logit Lens

Here we provide more fine-grained versions of the logit-lens analyses shown in the main paper. First, we group candidate words in other languages by their relationship to the translation task (source word, English, languages sharing the target script group, or languages with a different script group), which highlights how concepts develop language-(in)dependently Second, we group translation candidates by token overlap between the source and target words (no overlap, partial overlap, identical tokens). This view isolates how token overlap aids translation.

Figs. 14 and 13 provide more fine-grained versions of Fig. 3(b), while Figs. 15 and 16 show the corresponding layer-wise views at selected training checkpoints, complementing Fig. 5.

F.2 Copy Ablation
